hints.hint: Keep the candidate set finite and apply announcements in chronological order, recomputing information sets after each. Critical: if a displayed number is not labelled (e.g. could be the sum or the product), the speakers share that ambiguity, so a candidate is (my own value, which reading holds). "I don't know" then means my own value still admits two or more distinct partners, counting across readings; turn that into an arithmetic test on my own value (divisibility, positivity, range) and keep only values that pass. If every reading seems contradictory, you wrongly assumed the speakers knew the label. Never box a number just because it appeared in your enumeration: check the survivor satisfies every statement first.

Divide by the appropriate power of the variable to introduce the ratio w=(z-1)/z; the equation then pins w to a finite set on a circle. Solve for z in terms of w and turn the locus into an equation in x and y, completing the square to read off center and radius. Generally: substitute so the relation depends on one quantity, and keep every value exact.

A spot-check that disagrees with your derivation almost always means arithmetic inside the check, not a broken problem. Recheck that one line only; never restart from scratch or declare the setup inconsistent. Two exact points plus a symmetry axis pin a circle faster than solving a large linear system. State your simplified result as soon as you have one, then use leftover room to confirm it.

Fix coordinates once, pinned point at the origin; never restart the setup. For fixed-area pieces, union = sum minus overlap, so maximize the union by minimizing overlap. Beware the trap of assuming the bigger shape swallows the smaller one: a polygon vertex is only a wedge of its interior angle, so beyond that apex the shape covers nothing. Test one concrete point on the far side before concluding containment. When the apex sits at a center of n-fold rotational symmetry, that 2pi/n wedge cuts off exactly 1/n of the region at every rotation angle, so there is nothing to optimize. Then commit to one exact fraction and stop.

For "at most how many" extremal problems do both halves: an upper bound and a construction attaining it. Name a count early, before you run long.

Posit ONE unknown affine target for the whole pattern (an arithmetic progression is A+B*n), shared by every piece. Index n is then usable by piece f exactly when n is a root of f(x)-(A+Bx): a pointwise condition. Never demand that one piece's own consecutive difference be constant - neighbouring terms may come from different pieces, and that false identity is what makes the task look impossible.

Each such difference is a nonzero degree-d polynomial, so at most d roots. The root sets are disjoint and together fill the single progression, so budgets add: total <= (number of pieces) x d, already in the units asked for, not a per-piece cap.

Attain it by cutting the range into consecutive blocks, one piece interpolating each.

Name your unknowns and turn each given condition into one exact equation; solve for any constants first. Reduce to a single variable, keep exact fractions, and discard roots that are degenerate or outside the domain. Verify with a second, different method rather than repeating the first. State your result early, then stop.

Trap: asserting symmetry. "Each item is equally likely in any position", or "n! orderings so 1/n!", is a guess. A process random over MOVES is rarely uniform over OUTCOMES.

Instead build ONE sample space and reuse it for EVERY part. Its atoms are the genuinely FREE 50/50 choices: a step is 1/2 only when both options are legal, and forced steps count 1, so there are 2^(free) atoms — not 2^(all moves), not n!. First pin mechanics: which item a move may touch, and whether the asked slot is the FIRST or LAST arrival there.

Each part is then (atoms meeting its constraint)/2^(free). Later parts are where work drifts: never divide a permutation count by a branch count, and never retreat to 1/n. Calibrate on n=2.

Compute before theorizing. Replace the large size by n = 2, then 3; write that tiny system out and solve it exactly. Express each answer as a signed rational and factor it: 1/k!, a binomial, a product of differences. Two agreeing cases suggest the form; confirm on a third. Treat any structural claim ("the only solution is...", "that coefficient vanishes") as a guess and test it on n = 2 before building on it. If a derivation stalls or contradicts itself, abandon it rather than restarting -- the checked small cases already fix the pattern. State the closed form with its sign and index shift.

Let H be the total number of houses. The equal-street layout constrains H arithmetically, and integer stage costs per house mean H must divide every listed stage total. Determine the admissible common divisors using the intended maximum-feasible-count interpretation. Add all construction costs before dividing by H, apply the stated markup multiplicatively, and check integrality and units.

Never name a full set of unknown coefficients and never expand a composed or high-degree identity; that exhausts your budget. Recenter: put both maps about one shared unknown center c, f=c+a(x-c)^k and g=c-a(x-c)^k with odd k, so the identity collapses by symmetry. Take the opposite-sign branch first; same-sign is degenerate. Carry no extra offset and never factor c out. The two supplied values are then c-a*c^k and c+a*c^k: adding them must cancel the a-term, leaving one linear equation for c; subtracting isolates a. A quadratic or irrational center means your signs are wrong: fix that one line, never by expanding. Ask whether a requested input equals c or a fixed point, making its value immediate. Verify by symmetry, commit, state your result early, and stop re-deriving.

Trace concretely, not symbolically: write a row of distinct labels and rewrite the whole row after each stated step, each step acting on the previous row, never on the original. Never mix a "goes to" map with a "comes from" map. Any map you build by hand must be a bijection; if two inputs share an output, or one is missing, that is bookkeeping error, not exotic structure, so redo that trace. Return-to-start questions want an order: reapply the whole process, counting, until the row repeats. When the problem promises one formula in a parameter but your cases force a piecewise split, the odd case is almost surely mis-traced: recheck it, and trust the clean pattern rather than reporting a split or looping. Swap-shaped stages need not have period 2. Commit your result early, then stop.
